title: Analyses
blurb: The scripts that turn runs into tables.

blocks.lead: Run every analysis in dependency order, then the figures.

about.html: Each step runs one script from experiments/ in a separate process with the current Python interpreter and the current working directory. The run stops at the first step that fails, and each step's wall-clock time is printed as it finishes, with a summary at the end.

Three steps read the output of an earlier one: scaling_cost reads large_judges/small_vs_large.csv, and family_bias/student_ordering and significance/supplement read the family-bias matrices. The order runs those inputs first.
The significance steps build the cache of aligned correctness vectors in results/cache/significance/ the first time they run; later runs reuse it.

about.code:
examples, from the repository root:
  python experiments/run_all.py                  # every step
  python experiments/run_all.py --list           # print the steps and stop
  python experiments/run_all.py --from family_bias
  python experiments/run_all.py --only significance/all_pairs

about.html: Results are read from results/ (or $SLMJURY_RESULTS, which the child processes inherit) and written to results/analysis/<experiment>/ (tables) and results/figures/ (plots and figures).

actions.help: print the steps in order and stop
start at this step and run the rest

blocks.lead: Run-to-run variance: how often two runs of the same judge give different verdicts.

about.html: The token-budget single-factor study runs its own baseline conditions (baseline_t10 and baseline_t8192), with the same prompts, items and code as the original individual-judge runs. Comparing the two runs item by item shows how reproducible each judge's verdicts are.

Greedy decoding with vLLM is not fully deterministic. Continuous batching changes the order of floating-point reductions, so a token whose top two logits are nearly tied can go either way, and one changed token changes the rest of the generation. Confident judges are affected little, unsure judges more.

Judges with enable_thinking in slmjury/configs/models.yaml sample at temperature 0.6 at 8,192 tokens, so their rows at that budget are labelled "sampled". At 10 tokens thinking is off for every judge and decoding is greedy.

Reads: results/core/judgements/<judge>/<student>_<dataset>_t<budget>.json results/token_budget/single_factor/<judge>/baseline_t<budget>/<student>_<dataset>.json Writes: results/analysis/main_results/run_variance.csv
Run it from the repository root.

blocks.lead: Debate persuasion: when the agents disagree at the start, how often does a right answer lose?

about.html: Debate can only change items where the three agents open with different verdicts; when all three agree, the protocol stops. Among those items, this counts the ones where at least one agent was right at the outset, and reports the share that still ended with the wrong final verdict.
Only same-model configurations are counted (one model at three temperatures, names containing "-t0+"), so differences in agent capability do not affect the result.
Reads:  results/core/debate/<configuration>/<student>_<dataset>.json Writes: results/analysis/main_results/debate_persuasion.csv
Run it from the repository root.

blocks.lead: Small vs. large judges: accuracy, open-ended correlation and the scaling ladder.

about.html: Compares the sixteen small judges with six large judges (70B-122B) and the Qwen3-32B ladder judge on the same students and datasets. Large-judge accuracy is counted from the per-item judgement files with slmjury.analysis.accuracy and micro-averaged; small-judge accuracy comes from the per-judge summaries written by scripts/run_evaluation.py.
Each row records how many datasets it covers. complete_8ds marks the rows that cover all eight datasets and so can be compared directly.

Reads (under results/, or $SLMJURY_RESULTS): large_judges/<judge>/<student>_<dataset>_t<budget>.json large_judges/scoring_evaluations/<judge>/*_eval.json core/summaries/individual/<judge>_t<budget>.json core/scoring_evaluations/<judge>/*_eval.json

  small_vs_large.csv        one row per judge: accuracy per budget, best budget, correlations
  per_dataset.csv           judge x budget x dataset accuracy, two decimals

about.html: Cost model. Serving cost per judgement:

The same $0.55 per GPU-hour is applied to the small judges' 32 GB V100s and the large judges' 44 GiB cards. n_gpus is each judge's tensor_parallel_size in slmjury/configs/models.yaml (judge_models and large_judge_models), the GPU count the cost model assumes for 16-bit serving. blocks.lead: Token budget: the accuracy curve from 10 to 8,192 tokens, and the single-factor split.

about.html: Two analyses of the closed-ended verdicts:

items: Budget sweep. Accuracy per judge, dataset and budget for nine budgets, and per judge and budget over all of its datasets.

Single factor. Accuracy under each condition of run_single_factor.py, and its change from the 10-token baseline. Each condition changes one factor (budget, prompt, thinking or temperature), so the change shows what that factor alone does. A judge is scored on the datasets that every one of its conditions has, so a condition with more datasets cannot shift its own delta.

about.html: Datasets are found on disk. Accuracy is counted from the per-item judgement files with slmjury.analysis.accuracy and micro-averaged over students and datasets. Rates in the CSVs are computed from the integer counts and rounded once, to six decimals.
Reads (under results/, or $SLMJURY_RESULTS): token_budget/budget_sweep/<judge>/<student>_<dataset>_b<budget>.json token_budget/single_factor/<judge>/<condition>/<student>_<dataset>.json

about.code:
Writes results/analysis/token_budget/:
  budget_sweep.csv            judge x dataset accuracy at each budget
  budget_sweep_overall.csv    judge accuracy at each budget, micro-averaged over datasets
  single_factor_table.csv     judge x condition accuracy, IFR and change from baseline_t10
  single_factor_coverage.csv  the conditions and common datasets of each judge

about.html: experiments/adaptive_budget/analyze.py reads the same budget sweep.

The two runners in this folder judge the two main students (qwen2.5-32b, llama3.1-8b) on all eight closed-ended datasets; docs/REPRODUCE.md has the commands. The results cover fourteen of the sixteen small judges, all but phi4r-14b and phi4rp-14b. phi4mr-3.8b always thinks, so it has no 10-token budget and runs three of the six single-factor conditions.
Run it from the repository root.

blocks.lead: Adaptive budget: how cheap can a judge be without losing accuracy?

about.html: Uses the token-budget sweep to compare four ways of choosing a judge's budget:

about.code:
always_t10              10 tokens for every item
always_t8192            8,192 tokens for every item
domain_heuristic        one budget per answer type (numeric, latex,
                        multiple_choice): the median knee budget of that
                        type, rounded up to a swept budget
confidence_escalation   10 tokens, and a retry at 256 tokens for each item
                        whose 10-token verdict is Undefined

about.html: The knee of a judge x dataset curve is the smallest budget whose accuracy is within 0.5 points of the best budget for that cell.

Escalation is simulated item by item: the 256-token verdict replaces the 10-token verdict only on the items that were Undefined, and the result is scored like any other run. Every item pays the 10-token attempt, and each retried item also pays the 256-token retry. Cost is relative to always_t8192 (budget / 8,192 per item), averaged over items. Accuracy is micro-averaged over judges, students and datasets.
Judges that always think (phi4r-14b, phi4rp-14b, phi4mr-3.8b) have no 10-token budget, so no policy that starts at 10 tokens applies to them, and they are left out.
Reads (under results/, or $SLMJURY_RESULTS), with no new runs needed: token_budget/budget_sweep/<judge>/<student>_<dataset>_b<budget>.json (written by experiments/token_budget/run_budget_sweep.py)

about.code:
Writes results/analysis/adaptive_budget/:
  knee_budgets.csv                 judge x dataset: knee budget and accuracy at each budget
  domain_heuristic.json            the per-domain budgets the heuristic policy uses
  policy_comparison.csv            the four policies over all judges
  policy_comparison_by_judge.csv   the four policies per judge
and the plots, to results/figures/analysis/adaptive_budget/ (needs matplotlib):
  policy_comparison.png            accuracy and cost of each policy
  budget_curves.png                accuracy against budget per dataset

about.html: Run it from the repository root.

blocks.lead: Prompt sensitivity: how much does a judge's accuracy move when only the prompt wording changes?

about.html: Each judge graded the two main students under seven prompt variants (see slmjury/configs/prompt_variants.yaml). Five of them (original, minimal, gpt_style, rubric_based, cot_style) form the main comparison; adversarial and few_shot are stress tests reported against original.
Two rules keep the comparison fair:

items: Accuracy is micro-averaged, sum(correct) / sum(items) over files, as generate_judge_summary does. Averaging per-file accuracies would give small datasets (TruthfulQA, 684 items) the same weight as large ones (ARC-Easy, 2,376).

Variants are compared on common cells. For each judge, only the (student, dataset) cells present under every variant are scored. Otherwise a judge with 32 files under one variant and 7 under another would show a difference that comes from coverage, not from the prompt.

about.html: Reads (under results/, or $SLMJURY_RESULTS): prompt_sensitivity/<variant>/<judge>/<student>_<dataset>_t<budget>.json

about.code:
Writes results/analysis/prompt_sensitivity/:
  accuracy_table.csv          judge x budget accuracy per variant and the range,
                              each judge on its own common cells; stress
                              variants appear as extra rows (variant_group)
  shared_accuracy_table.csv   the judges with all five main variants, scored on
                              the cells every such judge shares, so all rows
                              are on the same items
  rank_stability.csv          mean and minimum pairwise Kendall tau between the
                              judge rankings the five main variants give
  stress_variants.csv         adversarial and few_shot against original, with
                              the unparseable share beside each accuracy, so a
                              formatting failure can be told from a wrong verdict
  coverage.csv                which cells each judge has under each variant

about.html: The runs come from run_prompt_variants.py in this folder, once per small judge and variant (docs/REPRODUCE.md has the commands). Its verdicts are read here; its SummEval and MT-Bench scores are read by analyze_open_ended.py.
Run it from the repository root.

Reads (under results/, or $SLMJURY_RESULTS): prompt_sensitivity/<variant>/<judge>/{summeval,mtbench_<reference>_<student>}.json prompt_sensitivity/<variant>/scoring_evaluations/<judge>/*_eval.json

blocks.lead: Judging protocols: do the verdicts hold up when the protocol changes?

about.html: Compares four ways of asking a judge about the same student answers on the eight closed-ended datasets:

about.code:
reference_based   the package's own prompts (results/core/judgements, and
                  results/large_judges for the large judges)
reference_free    the ground truth is left out of the prompt
geval             a 1-10 score thresholded at 7; 8,192 tokens only
pairwise          two students' answers side by side, in both orders

about.html: Only reference_free removes the ground truth. G-Eval and pairwise still show it and change the form of the answer.

For the first three, accuracy and instruction-following rate are counted from the per-item judgement files with slmjury.analysis.accuracy and micro-averaged over students and datasets. The reference-based row is counted here too, from the same files as the main results, so every protocol is scored by the same code.

For pairwise, every stored response is read again with slmjury.analysis.pairwise.read_choice (the stored verdict field is not used), and the flip rate is the share of items whose pick changes with the answer order, among items with an A or B in both orders. 0.5 is what random picks give. budget_invariant marks cells whose forward choices are the same at 10 and 8,192 tokens: the prompt asks for one letter, so a judge that does not think gives the same answer at both budgets, and the two cells are one measurement.

about.code:
Reads (under results/, or $SLMJURY_RESULTS):
  judging_protocols/referencefree/<judge>/<student>_<dataset>_t<budget>.json
  judging_protocols/geval/<judge>/<student>_<dataset>_t<budget>.json
  judging_protocols/pairwise/<judge>/<a>_vs_<b>_<dataset>_t<budget>_{fwd,rev}.json
  core/judgements/<judge>/<student>_<dataset>_t<budget>.json
  large_judges/<judge>/<student>_<dataset>_t<budget>.json    (if present)

Writes results/analysis/judging_protocols/:
  protocol_comparison.csv    judge x protocol: accuracy and IFR at each budget
  protocol_per_dataset.csv   judge x protocol x budget x dataset
  pairwise_flip_rate.csv     judge x pair x dataset x budget: flip rate and parse rate
  pairwise_summary.csv       judge x budget: mean, min and max flip rate

about.html: The three protocol runners in this folder judged the two main students (qwen2.5-32b, llama3.1-8b) on all eight datasets, for the sixteen small judges and for qwen2.5-72b and gpt-oss-120b; docs/REPRODUCE.md has the commands. The reference-based rows need the original judgements (scripts/run_judge.py) for the small judges and experiments/large_judges for the large ones.
Run it from the repository root.

blocks.lead: Family bias: does a judge grade students from its own model family more leniently?

about.html: Every judge grades a panel of students from several model families. For each judge and student the script computes

about.code:
FAR  = P(judge says Correct   | expected verdict is Incorrect)   leniency
FRR  = P(judge says Incorrect | expected verdict is Correct)     strictness

about.html: and accuracy. A judge family that favours its own lineage would show a higher FAR on same-family students than on the others. The expected verdict for each item comes from that item's own record in the judgement file, so nothing is joined by position across files.

Panels. Coverage is uneven, so the results are reported as five panels. Each one is a complete rectangle: every judge in it has a judgement for every student, dataset and budget the panel reports, and no cell is imputed.

about.code:
panel                            judges x students x datasets x budgets
eight_datasets_non_phi4_judges     11   x  5 (+1) x    8     x   2
eight_datasets                     13   x  5      x    8     x   2
eight_datasets_all_judges          16   x  5      x    8     x   1
five_datasets                      13   x  7      x    5     x   2
five_datasets_all_judges           16   x  7      x    5     x   1

about.html: eight_datasets is the largest complete rectangle at both budgets, and five_datasets holds every student. The two *_all_judges panels add the three Phi-4 reasoning judges, at 8,192 tokens only. eight_datasets_non_phi4_judges keeps the eleven judges outside the Phi-4 family, the only judges that graded qwen3-14b-student (the +1).

Two limits set these shapes. Three Phi-4 reasoning judges always think before answering and have no 10-token configuration, so a panel with both budgets holds 13 of the 16 judges. Two students (glm-4.7-flash, qwen3.5-35b-student) were generated on 5 datasets rather than 8, so an 8-dataset panel holds 5 of the 7 students.

qwen3-14b-student is a strong Qwen3 student, added because the other Qwen3 students are weak and lineage could not be separated from answer quality. It is marked with origin "probe" and joins a panel only when every cell of that panel exists for it; with the current results that is eight_datasets_non_phi4_judges. A student that has been judged only in part is listed on the console instead.

about.code:
Reads (under results/, or $SLMJURY_RESULTS):
  family_bias/judgements/<judge>/<student>_<dataset>_t<budget>.json
  core/judgements/<judge>/<student>_<dataset>_t<budget>.json         (qwen2.5-32b, llama3.1-8b)
  family_bias/student_solutions/<student>/<dataset>.json
  core/student_solutions/<student>/<dataset>.json                    (qwen2.5-32b, llama3.1-8b)

Writes results/analysis/family_bias/, for each panel

_false_accept_rate_matrix_t.csv FAR per judge x student

_false_reject_rate_matrix_t.csv FRR per judge x student

_accuracy_matrix_t.csv accuracy per judge x student

_family_summary.csv mean FAR on same-family vs. other students

_student_solver_accuracy.csv how often each student solved the item itself

about.html: experiments/family_bias/student_ordering.py reads the eight_datasets and five_datasets tables. docs/REPRODUCE.md lists the runs behind them (students and judgements). Run it from the repository root.

blocks.lead: Do judges agree on how to rank the students?

about.html: If leniency were a family effect, a Qwen judge would place a Qwen-lineage student higher than a Llama judge does. This script measures the orderings directly, for the eight_datasets and five_datasets panels at both budgets.
Two orderings are read from the family-bias matrices:

about.code:
accuracy            each judge's students from easiest to hardest to grade;
                    this is the ordering that should follow the students'
                    own solver accuracy
false_accept_rate   each judge's students from the one it is strictest with
                    to the one it is most lenient with

about.html: Agreement is Kendall's tau between the orderings of two judges, averaged over every pair of judges. The last column compares each judge's ordering with the students' solver accuracy and averages over judges. Every ordering is a ranking without ties, so tau-a (slmjury.analysis.metrics.kendall_tau) is the usual tau-b.

Reads results/analysis/family_bias/ (written by analyze.py in this folder): {eight_datasets,five_datasets}_student_solver_accuracy.csv {eight_datasets,five_datasets}_{accuracy,false_accept_rate}_matrix_t{10,8192}.csv
Writes results/analysis/family_bias/student_ordering.csv
Run it from the repository root, after analyze.py.

blocks.lead: Error analysis: what kind of mistake does each judge make?

about.html: Every item where a judge's verdict disagrees with the expected verdict, or where the verdict did not parse, is a disagreement. Each one is sorted into a category by rules, checked in this order:

about.code:
INSTRUCTION_FAILURE        the verdict did not parse (Correct/Incorrect missing)
CRITICAL_THINKING_FAILURE  the ground truth is empty or "None" (GSM-Plus items
                           with no valid answer)
FORMAT_MISMATCH            no student answer could be extracted, or a
                           multiple-choice answer uses letters where the ground
                           truth uses numbers (or the reverse)
SEMANTIC_EQUIVALENCE       the answers match under a lenient comparison, or are
                           numerically close and the judge accepted them
HALLUCINATED_COMPARISON    the judge's verdict contradicts a plain comparison of
                           the two answers
REASONING_DISTRACTION      the judge's response talks about the student's
                           reasoning or method
UNCLASSIFIED               none of the above

about.html: PARTIAL_CREDIT has a column in the output, but no rule assigns it. The lenient comparisons only sort disagreements into categories. The expected verdict itself comes from slmjury.analysis.accuracy.expected_verdict, the same rule JudgeEvaluator uses.

The error distribution covers the sixteen small judges and, when their results are present, the large judges and the Qwen3-32B ladder judge, all through the same code. Phi-4 (phi4-14b) also gets a full list of its disagreements and a chart by answer type.

Reads (under results/, or $SLMJURY_RESULTS), with no new runs needed:
  core/judgements/<judge>/<student>_<dataset>_t<budget>.json    (scripts/run_judge.py)
  large_judges/<judge>/<student>_<dataset>_t<budget>.json       (if present)

Writes results/analysis/error_analysis/:
  error_distribution.csv          per judge: disagreement counts, direction and category
  disagreements_phi4-14b.csv      every disagreement of phi4-14b, with truncated texts
and the plots, to results/figures/analysis/error_analysis/ (needs matplotlib):

  fp_fn_by_domain_phi4-14b.png    phi4-14b errors by answer type

blocks.lead: Significance tests and confidence intervals for the judge comparisons.

about.html: Every closed-ended comparison is paired: two judges are compared on the same 64,824 items (two students, eight datasets), using the aligned correctness vectors from data.py. The tests are:

about.code:
McNemar            exact two-sided test on the discordant items
cluster bootstrap  95% CI on the accuracy difference, items resampled
                   within each dataset (10,000 resamples)
TOST               two one-sided tests for equivalence within +-0.5 points
Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate q-values over all judge pairs
Wilson interval    for a single proportion (accuracy, extraction failures)
Spearman bootstrap 95% CI on a correlation, pairs resampled together

about.html: Each judge is used at its better budget (10 or 8,192 tokens). The script has three parts, each writing complete tables on its own; by default it runs all three in order.

about.code:
small-vs-large
  paired_tests.csv              each large judge against the five best small
                                judges: McNemar, bootstrap CI, TOST, micro and
                                macro accuracy
  mtbench_common_reference.csv  MT-Bench correlation per judge, averaged three
                                ways: over every reference model except the
                                judge itself (rho_all_refs), over the one
                                reference that is not also a judge
                                (rho_common_ref, qwen3.5-397b), and with both
                                students pooled into one correlation with a
                                bootstrap CI
  extraction_accounting.csv/.json
                                items whose student answer cannot be
                                extracted, per student and dataset; they are
                                scored Incorrect and stay in the denominator
all-pairs
  paired_tests_all_pairs.csv    every pair of the 22 judges (231 pairs), with
                                BH q-values
  tost_equivalence.csv          the TOST columns of the same pairs
  macro_vs_micro.csv            micro and macro accuracy, Wilson interval and
                                IFR for every judge and budget
  open_ended_ci.csv             bootstrap CIs on every SummEval and MT-Bench
                                correlation (dimensions and students pooled)
open-ended
  summeval_paired.csv           the five best small judges (by closed-ended
                                accuracy) against each large judge on SummEval,
                                paired, with articles resampled
  mtbench_reference_agreement.csv/.json
                                Spearman correlation between the two MT-Bench
                                reference models, per student, with a CI
  reference_free_penalty_by_size.csv/.json
                                accuracy lost without the reference answer,
                                per judge, and its rank correlation with size

Reads (under results/, or $SLMJURY_RESULTS):
  core/judgements/, large_judges/         per-item verdicts (through data.py)
  core/scoring/<judge>/, large_judges/<judge>/
                                          per-item SummEval and MT-Bench scores
  core/scoring_evaluations/<judge>/, large_judges/scoring_evaluations/<judge>/

blocks.lead: Aligned per-item correctness vectors for the significance tests.

about.html: Every test in this folder compares two judges on the same items, so both judges' results have to describe the same items in the same order. This module does that alignment once, and the analysis scripts import it.

items: A judge is correct on an item when its verdict matches the expected verdict from slmjury.analysis.accuracy.expected_verdict, the same rule JudgeEvaluator uses (MATH answers are compared through the shipped label table). An Undefined verdict counts as wrong and the item stays in the denominator, so accuracies here equal the per-judge accuracies elsewhere.
Items are keyed by (student, dataset, problem_id). Every judgement file must carry the same ordered id list as the item index; a mismatch raises an error instead of comparing different items.
Small judges are read from results/core/judgements, large and ladder judges from results/large_judges.

blocks.lead: Confidence intervals on the reported open-ended correlations.

about.html: analyze.py bootstraps pooled correlations (SummEval with the four dimensions pooled, MT-Bench with both students pooled). The reported statistics are different: SummEval rho is the mean of the four per-dimension Spearman correlations, and MT-Bench rho on the common reference model (qwen3.5-397b) is the mean of the two per-student correlations. This script bootstraps those statistics, after checking that each point estimate matches the stored evaluation files.

Every judge is resampled with the same draws, so the difference between two judges gets a paired interval. Point estimates are computed without intermediate rounding (slmjury.analysis.scoring), and values are written to six decimals so that rounding them to three for a table rounds only once.
The 22 judges of analyze.py are joined by the Qwen3-32B ladder judge.

Reads (under results/, or $SLMJURY_RESULTS): core/scoring/<judge>/, large_judges/<judge>/ summeval.json, mtbench_qwen3.5-397b_<student>.json core/scoring_evaluations/<judge>/, large_judges/scoring_evaluations/<judge>/ mtbench_qwen3.5-397b_<student>_eval.json

about.html: ladder_paired.csv The Qwen3 scaling ladder (0.6B to 122B), each rung against the one below it, plus Qwen3-32B against Phi-4. Each judge is used at its better budget and both are compared on the same items: exact McNemar test, cluster bootstrap 95% CI on the accuracy difference (10,000 resamples within datasets) and TOST for equivalence within +-0.5 points.
